analysis.title: Global Economics Daily Points, October 30, 2026
key_insights: US stock futures are down 1% (S&P) to over 2% (Nasdaq) after after-market earnings misses from Intel and Amazon, which followed Alphabet's earlier miss. The misses spanned EPS, revenue and revenue guidance.

Oil is up about 2%+ with WTI at $104 and Brent above US$117, after WSJ headlines that war plans against Iran are afoot and Trump has been briefed on attack options. A 'short, intense campaign' has been guided.
The dollar is not attracting safe haven flows. Every major currency is rallying against it.

Pricing for a December FOMC hike has fallen from nearly fully priced a couple of days ago to about 18bps of a quarter-point hike. Scotiabank questions this direction given higher oil and how Warsh may view inflation. US Treasuries are rallying in a slight bull steepener.

The Bank of Japan kept December hike pricing intact at about 20bps of a quarter-point hike, with 1-2 more hikes into next summer. The core CPI forecast for 2027 was raised two-tenths to 2.6% and 2026 held at 2.5%.

Governor Ueda said every meeting is live, including the next one. He chose not to lean against December hike pricing, and said the BoJ has achieved its 2% target with upside risk, a slight upgrade from 'getting close'.
Canada August GDP is expected at 0.2% m/m, with a first September estimate (no details) due. Q3 growth is tracked at about 2% q/q SAAR. September may be weak given the drop in hours worked.
Scotiabank says the BoC was right to hike and that the doves who failed to predict tightening are replaying their song book.
Eurozone Q3 GDP grew 0.4% q/q versus 0.2% consensus, after 0.6% in Q2. Spain led at 0.6%, Germany 0.2%, Italy flat and France -0.1%.

Eurozone October inflation consensus of 0.3% m/m looks light given national data: France 0.4% (0.3% consensus), Spain 0.5% (in line), Italy 1.2% (0.4% consensus). German state CPIs at 0% to -0.3% m/m track below the 0.1% consensus.
Spain's core CPI was weaker than normal for an October.
Colombia's central bank is split ahead of its 2pm ET decision: slightly more than half expect a hold at 12.25% and slightly fewer expect a 25bp hike.
Mexico Q3 GDP is expected at about 1% q/q after 1.4% in Q2, with estimates ranging from scant growth to 1.75%.
US Employment Cost Index for Q3 is expected at 0.8% q/q consensus (Scotiabank 0.9%, prior 0.9%), running well above the Fed's 2% target on an annualized basis.

risk_factors: Escalation of US military action against Iran and higher oil prices adding to inflation.
Tech earnings misses from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel spreading across the sector.
Oil flaring may add to how Warsh views inflation, making the market's reduced December FOMC hike pricing look too low.
Canada September GDP may be weak given the drop in hours worked.
Eurozone October inflation could surprise on the upside given France and Italy, but German states point lower.
charts_described: Chart 3 shows Canada Q3 GDP tracking at +2.0% q/q SAAR.
Chart 1 plots the US Employment Cost Index q/q change, SA annualized, as rising at a steady pace well above the Fed's 2% target but well off the pandemic peak.
vol_and_positioning: The dollar is not gaining safe haven flows despite the risk-off tone, with every major currency rallying against it.
US Treasuries are rallying in a slight bull steepener, and most other global benchmarks are slightly dearer. JGBs rallied in a bull flattener, which the author links to global risk aversion.
geopolitical: WSJ reported that US war plans are afoot and Trump has been briefed on attack options against Iran. A 'short, intense campaign' has been guided, and the author compares it to about nine months ago.
Higher oil prices on signs of a major US escalation against Iran are weighing on risk appetite.

tension_points.bull_case: Markets have cut December hike odds to about 18bps as the tech wreck damages risk appetite.
tension_points.bear_case: Scotiabank is not sure the direction is correct, since oil is flaring and adds to how Warsh may view inflation.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further oil gains or firm inflation data, such as the Employment Cost Index, would push hike pricing back up.
